title: Computing the standard error of the estimate from ANOVA residual sum of squares
scenario_markdown:
A manufacturing cost analyst estimates weekly overhead maintenance expense ($Y$, in thousands of dollars) from total direct machine operating hours ($X$, in hundreds of hours) across $n = 20$ manufacturing facilities. The Excel regression summary output ANOVA table reports:

| ANOVA Source | $df$ | $SS$ | $MS$ | $F$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Regression | $1$ | $1{,}024.0$ | $1{,}024.0$ | $64.0$ |
| Residual | $18$ | $288.0$ | ? | |
| Total | $19$ | $1{,}312.0$ | | |

Coefficients: Intercept $b_0 = 15.0$ ($SE = 2.5$), Direct Labor Hours $b_1 = 3.20$ ($SE = 0.40$). Calculate the mean squared error ($MSE$), the standard error of the regression estimate ($s_e$), and interpret $s_e$ in business terms.
assumptions: Simple linear regression model with k = 1 predictor and sample size n = 20
Residual degrees of freedom df_residual = n - 2 = 18
Standard error of estimate s_e = sqrt(MSE) is expressed in the units of Y (thousands of dollars)

approval.notes: Reviewed derivation: n = 20, k = 1, SSR = 1024.0, SSE = 288.0, SST = 1312.0. df_res = 20 - 2 = 18. MSE = 288.0 / 18 = 16.0. Standard error of estimate s_e = sqrt(16.0) = 4.0 ($4,000). Consistency check: F = 1024/16 = 64.0; t_slope = 3.2/0.4 = 8.0 -> t^2 = 64.0 == F exactly. Excel: =SQRT(288/18).

stages.prompt_markdown: Determine the residual degrees of freedom and compute the mean squared error ($MSE = \frac{SSE}{n - 2}$).

options.hint_markdown: In simple linear regression, two parameters ($b_0$ and $b_1$) are estimated from the data, so residual degrees of freedom are $n - 2 = 20 - 2 = 18$, not $n = 20$.
$19$ is the total degrees of freedom ($n - 1$); the residual row has $n - k - 1 = 18$ degrees of freedom.
Mean squared error is the residual sum of squares divided by residual degrees of freedom: $288.0 / 18 = 16.0$.

stages.explanation_markdown: In a simple linear regression ($k = 1$), the residual degrees of freedom are $df_{\text{res}} = n - k - 1 = 20 - 1 - 1 = 18$. The mean squared error is: $$MSE = \frac{SSE}{df_{\text{res}}} = \frac{288.0}{18} = 16.0$$

stages.prompt_markdown: Compute the standard error of the estimate $s_e = \sqrt{MSE}$.

options.hint_markdown: The standard error of the estimate is the square root of $MSE$: $\sqrt{16.0} = 4.0$.
$s_e$ evaluates unexplained residual variance ($SSE / 18$), not total sample variance ($SST / 19$).
$78.05\%$ is $R^2 = SSR / SST$; $s_e$ is an absolute dispersion metric in the original units of $y$.

stages.explanation_markdown: The standard error of the estimate (often called the standard error of the regression, or $s_e$) is: $$s_e = \sqrt{MSE} = \sqrt{16.0} = 4.0\text{ (thousands of dollars, or } \$4{,}000\text{)}$$

stages.prompt_markdown: How should managers interpret the numerical value $s_e = 4.0$ in decision-making?

options.text_markdown: Observed weekly overhead costs deviate from model predictions by roughly $\$4,000$ on average.
The estimated slope changes by $\$4,000$ across different samples.
options.hint_markdown: The standard error of the slope is $s_{b_1} = 0.40$; $s_e = 4.0$ measures typical prediction error around the regression line.

options.text_markdown: The maximum possible prediction error the model can ever make is exactly $\$4,000$.
options.hint_markdown: $s_e$ is a standard deviation of residuals, not an absolute upper bound on individual residuals.

options.text_markdown: The model explains $4\%$ of the variation in weekly overhead costs.
options.hint_markdown: Explained variance is measured by $R^2 = 78.05\%$, not $s_e$.

stages.explanation_markdown: The standard error of the regression $s_e = \$4{,}000$ provides an intuitive gauge of model accuracy. It represents the approximate standard deviation of the residuals—meaning observed weekly maintenance costs typically fall within about $\pm \$4{,}000$ of the fitted regression line.
